Real-Time Retail Feedback Intelligence

Business Context¶

ChicStyle is a rapidly growing online fashion platform specializing in women's clothing and accessories. During the peak shopping season, the platform receives an overwhelming volume of customer reviews. These unstructure text reviews contains postive comments, complaints about product quality, delivery delays, incorrect sizes, damaged products or dissatifaction with colors and fitting. Manually reading, tagging and synthesizing thousands of review is not scalable and time consuming.

Traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) have significant limitations because they depend on fixed rules and limited training data. These systems often fail to understand complex customer reviews that contains mixed opinions.

Modern Generative AI models are deeply capable of understanding full meaning of customer feedback, detect mixed emotions and separate opinions related to different product features more effectively.

Objective¶

The primary objective of this project is to develop a real-time feedback intelligence system. The workflow is divided into four major analytical phases.

  1. Exploratory Data Analysis : Perform EDA to uncover key patterns and insights in the dataset before applying any AI techniques.

  2. Generative AI Pipeline Engineering : It then applies Large Language Model(LLM) to extract structured intelligence from customer reviews such as category, sentiment, summary, suggested reply and insights using Zero-Shot, Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought prompting methods.

  3. Validation : The project further evaluates and compares these prompting strategies through an LLM-as-Judge scoring framework to determine their effectiveness. Additionally, it classifies whether customers would recommend the product and assesses prediction accuracy.

  4. Actionable Strategy Formulation : Finally, it translates the findings into actionable business recommendations to improve customer experience and product strategy.

Data Dictionary¶

This analysis uses the "Women's E-Commerce Clothing Reviews" dataset. The key columns for the analysis are:

  • Clothing.ID : A unique ID for each piece of clothing (Postive Integer).
  • Age : The age of the reviewer (Positive Integer).
  • Title: The title of the review (String).
  • Review.Text : The main body of the customer's reviewtext (String).
  • Rating : The product score given by the customer, from 1(Worst) to 5(Best) (Positive Ordinal Integer).
  • Recommended.IND : A binary variable indicating if the customer recommends the product (1 for recommended, 0 for not recommended).
  • Positive.Feedback.Count : The number of other customers who found the review helpful (Positive Integer).
  • Division.Name: The high-level division of the product (Categorical).
  • Department.Name: The specific department of the product (Categorical).

Observation

  • Approximately 16% (3810) reviews have missing values in the 'Title' column. This suggest that many customer tend to bypass the optional title field and provide their review directly in the main review text section.
  • The 'Review.Text' column has 845 missing data(3.6% of the dataset). This suggest that some customers provide the ratings but chose not to leave any written reviews.
  • The 'Division', 'Department' and 'Class' has 14 missing values of data (0.06% of the dataset). Notably, one customer skipped all the optional field and provided only a rating, while remaining 13 customers omitted one or two of the 'Division','Department' or 'Class' column.
  • The dataset contains 21 duplicate records. This may be due to multiple submissions by the customer or duplication during data processing. The exact reason cannot be determined by the data alone.

Data Cleaning and Preprocessing¶

Think about it: The Review Text column is the most critical feature for our Generative AI model. What should be done with rows where this text is missing?

In [508]:
# Step 1: Drop the 21 duplicate rows from the dataset
df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)

# Check the duplicate rows are cleaned
print(f"Duplicate Rows  : {df.duplicated().sum()}")

# Shape of the dataset after dropping the duplicate rows
print(f"Shape of the dataset after removing duplicates  : {df.shape[0]:,} rows")

Duplicate Rows  : 0
Shape of the dataset after removing duplicates  : 23,465 rows

Observation

  • The 21 duplicate records may be the result of multiple review submissions by the customer or duplication during data processing.
  • Given their smaller proportion, they are unlikely to have a significant impact on the analysis. Therefore, these duplicate records can be safely removed from the dataset.
In [509]:
# Step 2: Drop rows where Review.Text is missing( which essential for AI pipeline)
df.dropna(subset=['Review.Text'],inplace=True)

# Shape of the dataset after dropping the rows with missing Review.Text
print(f"Shape of the dataset after removing rows with missing reviews : {df.shape[0]:,} rows")

Shape of the dataset after removing rows with missing reviews : 22,640 rows

Observation

  • The column 'Review.Text' is a critical input for text based AI modelling. If the review has rating but not text, then the model has nothing to analyze.
  • Imputing the placeholder text like 'No Reviews' provides zero signal and wastes the API tokens. Therefore, dropping these rows are the cleanest approach.
In [510]:
# Step 3: Fill missing Title with empty string
df['Title']=df['Title'].fillna("")

Observation

  • Removing the rows with missing values of 'Title' column would result in the loss of a large number of otherwise valid reviews and ratings, which are important for the analysis.
  • Instead, imputing the missing Title values with empty string ("") ensures that all records are retained while helping the text processing algorithms to operate smoothly.
In [511]:
# Step 4: Fill missing Product hierarchy with 'Unknown'
for col in ["Division.Name","Department.Name","Class.Name"]:
  df[col]=df[col].fillna('Unknown')

Observation

  • Missing values in the 'Division.Name', 'Department.Name','Class.Name' column are filled with 'Unknown'.
  • This helps to retain all the records of the dataset for data analysis without losing valuable information.
In [512]:
# Step 5: Add a review length feature to help with the EDA
df["Review.Length"]=df["Review.Text"].str.len()

Observation

  • The length of the review often correlates strongly with the customer sentiment. For example, highly frustrated or highly satified customer often writes much longer explanation.
  • Hence adding this column to the dataset will helps us analyze the customer sentiment more efficiently

Univariate Analysis¶

In [516]:
# Function to plot a histogram and boxplot in the same page
def plt_hist_boxplot(df, feature, figsize=(12,7),kde=False,bins=None):
  """"
  Boxplot and Histogram Combined
  df : dataframe
  feature : column name
  figsize : size of the figure (default = (12,7))
  kde : Kernel Density Estimate (default = False)
  bins : bins for histogram (default = None)
  """
  f2,(ax2_box2,ax2_hist2)=plt.subplots(
      nrows=2, # No of rows of the subplot grid = 2
      sharex=True, # X-axis will be shared among all subplots
      gridspec_kw={"height_ratios":(0.25,0.75)},
      figsize=figsize
  )

  # Creating the 2 subplots - histogram and boxplot

  # Create the histogram for the dataset
  sns.histplot(
      data=df,
      x=feature,
      kde=kde,
      bins=bins,
      ax=ax2_hist2,

  ) if bins else sns.histplot(
      data=df,
      x=feature,
      kde=kde,
      ax=ax2_hist2,

  )
  # Add mean to the histogram plot
  ax2_hist2.axvline(
    df[feature].mean(),
    color="red",
    linestyle='--')

  # Add median to the histogram plot
  ax2_hist2.axvline(
      df[feature].median(),
      color="black",
      linestyle='-')

  # Create the boxplot and star will indicate the mean value of the dataset
  sns.boxplot(
      data=df,
      x=feature,
      ax=ax2_box2,
      showmeans=True,
      color="gold")

Observation

  • Age : The dataset include customers aged between 18-99 years. The age distribution is concentrated around the middle age group(median = 41 years), indicating that the products, design preferences and sizing language are likely tailored towards this demographic.

  • Rating : The ratings variable is constrained to values between 1 to 5 stars.The average rating is 4.18, indicating that most customer are happy. The summary shows a positive sentiment of 25th Percentile at 4.0 and 75th percentile at 5.0. The top 25% of the customers gave perfect 5 star rating while 75% of the customers gave 4.0 star or above rating. This shows overall the customer satisfaction is strong.

  • Recommended.IND : Recommended variable is a binary value of 0 or 1. The mean is 0.82. This implies that 82% of the customer would recommend the product, further supporting overall customer satisfaction.

  • Positive.Feedback.Count : Positive Feedback count has an average of 2.63. The count has minimum value of 0 and maximum value of 122. The median is 1, which means half of all the reviews get 1 or 0 helpful vote from the other shoppers. But there are few reviews which became viral and got a helpful vote of 122 thumbs up.

  • Review Length : The average Review Length is 309 characters, reviews ranging between 9 characters to 512 characters. This shows the variation in the level of details the customer provide when sharing the feedback.

  1. How many unique values are there in the categorical columns like Division Name, Department Name, and Class Name?

#Unique values in the "Division.Name", "Department.Name","Class.Name"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cat_cols = ["Division.Name","Department.Name","Class.Name"]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(16,11))

for ax,col in zip(axes,cat_cols):
  vc=df[col].value_counts()
  ax.barh(vc.index[::-1],vc.values[::-1],color=sns.color_palette("Set2",len(vc)),edgecolor="white")
  for i,v in enumerate(vc.values[::-1]):
    ax.text(v+30,i,f"{v:,}",va="center",fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(col.replace(".", " "), fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlabel("Number of Reviews")


plt.suptitle("Categorical Column Distributions", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14, y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation

  • Division Name : General dominates the dataset by 59% whereas Initmates is a small division of 0.06%.
  • Department : 'Tops' leads by 10,048 reviews. Followed by 'Dresses' with 6,145 reviews. This means 'Tops' and 'Dresses' are the core product lines.
  • Class Name : The dataset contains a total of 21 classes. The 'Dresses' and 'Knits' are the top two classes in the dataset. The class 'Casual Bottoms' and 'Chemises' have only one review and will not produce a reliable model signals.
  1. What is the overall distribution of product Rating? Is the dataset skewed towards positive or negative reviews?.
In [523]:
#Overall Distribution of Product Rating
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(16,11))
colors=["#E74C3C", "#E67E22", "#F1C40F", "#2ECC71", "#27AE60"]
rating_counts=df["Rating"].value_counts().sort_index()
# Bar chart
axes[0].bar(rating_counts.index,rating_counts.values,color=colors,edgecolor="white",linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Star Rating")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of Reviews")
axes[0].set_title("Rating Count by Star")
# Bar Chart
for i, v in enumerate(rating_counts.values):
  axes[0].text(i+1, # Positions the text exactly at the bar'center index
               v+100, # Offsets text slightly above the bar height
               f"{v:,}\n({100*v/rating_counts.sum():.1f}%)",
               ha="center",
               fontsize=9,
               fontweight="bold"
  )
#Pie Chart
axes[1].pie(rating_counts.values,labels=[f"{i}-Star" for i in rating_counts.index],
            autopct="%1.1f%%",colors=colors,startangle=90,
            wedgeprops={"edgecolor":"white","linewidth":1.5})
axes[1].set_title("Rating Share")


plt.suptitle("Overall Rating Distribution", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation

  • 5-Star Rating : Majority of the customers were highly satisfied contributing to 55.4% of customer reviews (12,539 reviews) of 5-star rating.
  • 4-Star Rating : Additionally 21.7%(4,908 reviews) of customers rated 4-star ratings in their reviews. This shows around 77.1% of reviews falls within positive ratings.
  • 3-Star Rating : Around 12.5%(2,823 reviews) of customer reviews were 3-Star. This reflects a smaller proportion of neutral customer experience.
  • 1-Star and 2-Star Rating : It contributes to 10.4% of 1-star(821 reviews) and 2-star(1,549 reviews) negative rating together.
  • Overall, the data set is heavily positive skewed indicating strong customer satisfaction. This shows a strong imbalance in the dataset. The models will only learn from the positive reviews. Hence the model should be judged based on accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score to identify the positive and negative reviews correctly.

# Data-Driven Stopword List
from collections import Counter

def tokenize(series):
  text=" ".join(series.astype(str).tolist()).lower()
  return re.findall(r"[a-z']+",text)

high_reviews =df[df["Rating"] >= 4]["Review.Text"]
low_reviews  =df[df["Rating"] <= 2]["Review.Text"]

high_words = [w for w in tokenize(high_reviews) if w not in STOPWORDS and len(w) > 2]
low_words  = [w for w in tokenize(low_reviews)  if w not in STOPWORDS and len(w) > 2]



high_freq,low_freq = Counter(high_words),Counter(low_words)
high_total,low_total=len(high_words),len(low_words) # normalize: groups have different sizes

# Look only at words common enough to matter (top 80 by raw frequency on either side)
candidates = set([w for w, _ in high_freq.most_common(80)]+[w for w, _ in low_freq.most_common(80)])

rows = []
for w in candidates:
    h_rate = high_freq.get(w, 0) / high_total * 1000   # occurrences per 1,000 words
    l_rate = low_freq.get(w, 0) / low_total * 1000
    skew = (h_rate - l_rate) / (h_rate + l_rate + 1e-6)
    rows.append((w, h_rate, l_rate, skew))

skew_df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["word", "high_rate_per_1k", "low_rate_per_1k", "skew"])

# Words with |skew| < 0.15 appear at roughly equal rates in both groups -> structural noise
NEUTRAL_THRESHOLD = 0.15
neutral_words = set(skew_df.loc[skew_df["skew"].abs() < NEUTRAL_THRESHOLD, "word"])

custom_stop = STOPWORDS | neutral_words

print(f"Data-driven stopwords added ({len(neutral_words)} words, |skew| < {NEUTRAL_THRESHOLD}):")
print(sorted(neutral_words))

print("\nFor comparison — the strongest SIGNAL words we are correctly keeping:")
print("\n  Skewed toward NEGATIVE reviews (keep!):")
print(" ", skew_df.sort_values("skew").head(8)["word"].tolist())
print("\n  Skewed toward POSITIVE reviews (keep!):")
print(" ", skew_df.sort_values("skew", ascending=False).head(8)["word"].tolist())

Data-driven stopwords added (34 words, |skew| < 0.15):
['beautiful', 'big', 'blue', 'color', 'cute', 'dress', 'fit', 'front', 'good', 'large', 'lbs', 'look', 'one', 'pants', 'pretty', 'really', 'retailer', 'right', 'runs', 'sale', 'see', 'skirt', 'sleeves', 'small', 'still', 'style', 'sweater', 'top', 'tried', 'usually', 'waist', 'wearing', 'white', 'work']

For comparison — the strongest SIGNAL words we are correctly keeping:

  Skewed toward NEGATIVE reviews (keep!):
  ['cheap', 'disappointed', 'huge', 'returned', 'unfortunately', 'looked', 'return', 'wanted']

  Skewed toward POSITIVE reviews (keep!):
  ['comfortable', 'perfectly', 'fits', 'perfect', 'fall', 'little', 'summer', 'jeans']

Observation

  • Words like 'beautiful', 'big', 'blue', 'color', 'cute', 'dress', 'fit', 'front', 'good', 'large' turns our to be genuinely neutral. They describe what is being reviewed, not how the customer feels confirming the intuition based guess was reasonable for these.
  • Words like 'comfortable', 'perfectly', 'fits', 'perfect', 'fall', 'little' are skewed positively
  • Words like 'cheap', 'disappointed', 'huge', 'returned', 'unfortunately', 'looked', 'return', 'wanted' are negatively skewed.
  • The Positively and Negatively skewed words are the words that need to be visible in the word cloud. They are filtered out only if they cross the neutral threshold ( < 0.15) but they wont. This risks the loss of words if intuition based guess is considered.

Building the Generative AI Pipeline¶

We will now build a system to analyze the reviews. This involves setting up the AI client, designing prompts, generating structured data, and evaluating the results.

Setup AI Client and Data Sample¶

Questions:

Note:¶

For this project, we will analyze and categorize a sample of 50 customer reviews. This number is chosen intentionally. Since the API has a budget limit of $20, running prompts on very large datasets can quickly exhaust your quota—especially because this exercise may involve multiple iterations, prompt refinements, and repeated evaluations.

To avoid unnecessary cost and ensure efficient experimentation, we recommend the following approach:

  • Use very small samples (5–10 reviews) during the initial testing phase to validate your prompt structure and logic.

  • Scale up to 50 reviews for the final evaluation phase, ensuring you get enough data to compare prompting techniques without draining your budget.

  • This strategy helps maintain cost control while still providing meaningful insights across Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought techniques.

If your API quota gets exhausted, you may temporarily switch to another free AI assistant API. However, note that external tools may also have rate limits or token caps, so you will need to build retry logic and manage throttling within your code.

np.random.seed(42)
parts=[]
for rating_value,group in df.groupby("Rating"):
  n_take=max(1,round(SAMPLE_SIZE*len(group)/len(df)))
  parts.append(group.sample(n=min(n_take,len(group)),random_state=42))

sample_df = pd.concat(parts,ignore_index=True)

if len(sample_df) > SAMPLE_SIZE:
  sample_df=sample_df.sample(n=SAMPLE_SIZE,random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)
elif len(sample_df) < SAMPLE_SIZE:
  extra = df.drop(sample_df.index).sample(n=SAMPLE_SIZE-len(sample_df),random_state=42)
  sample_df=pd.concat([sample_df,extra],ignore_index=True)

# Function : Send a text to OpenAI API and return the text response
def call_llm(prompt:str)->str:
  try:
    response=client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL_NAME,
        messages=[{"role":"user","content":prompt}],
        temperature=0.3,
        max_tokens=400,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
  except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error Calling OpenAI:{e}")
    return f"ERROR: {e}"
  return""
In [531]:
# Function :Extract the structure fields from a LLM response. Format as Field Name : Value
def parse_structured_output(text:str)->dict:
  fields = ["Category","Sentiment","Summary","Personalized Message","Retail Insight"]
  result={}
  for field in fields:
    pattern = rf"{field}\s*:\s*(.*?)(?=\n[A-Za-z ]+:|\Z)"
    match=re.search(pattern,text,re.DOTALL)
    result[field]=match.group(1).strip() if match else "N/A"
  return result

# LLM as Judge - to evaluate the quality of structured output
def llm_judge(review_text:str,generated_output:str,rating:int)->float:
  judge_prompt=f""" You are an expert evaluator for a retail AI system.
  Score the following AI-generated analysis of a customer review.

  ORIGINAL REVIEW (Rating :{rating}/5):
  \"{review_text}\"

  AI-GENERATED OUTPUT:
  {generated_output}

  Evaluate on these 5 criteria (each worth 0.2)
  1. All fields are present(Category, Sentiment, Summary, Personalized Message, Retail Insight)
  2. Sentiment matches the star rating
  3. Summary accurately reflects the review
  4. Personalized message is emphathetic and brand-appropiate
  5. Retail insight is specific and actionable

  Returns only the number between 0.0 and 1.0
  """
  raw=call_llm(judge_prompt)
  try:
    return round(float(re.search(r"[0-9]+\.?[0-9]*",raw).group()),3)
  except Exception:
    return 0.5

# Prompt pipeline
def run_prompt_pipeline(prompt_builder_fn,label: str)->tuple:
  rows=[]
  for idx, row in sample_df.iterrows():
    review,rating = row["Review.Text"],row["Rating"]
    prompt=prompt_builder_fn(review,rating)
    output=call_llm(prompt)
    score=llm_judge(review,output,rating)
    parsed=parse_structured_output(output)
    parsed.update({
        "Technique"  : label,
        "Review_Text": str(review)[:80]+"...",
        "Rating"     : rating,
        "Judge_Score": score,
        })
    rows.append(parsed)
   # time.sleep(0.2)

  df_out=pd.DataFrame(rows)
  avg   =round(df_out["Judge_Score"].mean(),4)
  print(f" {label :} avg judge score = {avg:.4f}")
  return df_out,avg

print("Pipeline runner defined")

Pipeline runner defined

Prompt Engineering and Evaluation¶

We will test three different prompting techniques. For each, we will create a basic version (V1) and an enhanced version (V2).

Think about it: Why is it important to have a consistent and robust evaluation framework? How can we use an "LLM-as-Judge" to score the quality of our generated outputs objectively?

Technique 1: Zero-Shot Prompting¶

Questions:

  1. How would you design a basic Zero-Shot prompt that asks the model for Category, Sentiment, Summary, Personalized Message, and Retail Insight?

  2. How can you enhance this prompt with more business context (e.g., a company name, the importance of accuracy) to create a V2 prompt?

  3. How will you loop through the data sample to generate and store the structured output for both prompt versions?

  4. How will you apply the LLM-as-Judge to generate a evaluation score between 0 to 1 (decimal allowed) for the outputs and calculate the average score of V1 and V2 prompt?

How the process works:

  1. First, you create an LLM-as-a-judge function that can evaluate the quality of model outputs.

  2. Then, you run your Zero-Shot Prompt Version 1 on a sample of 50 reviews to generate predictions.

  3. You use the judge function to score each prediction and compute the average score for Version 1.

  4. Next, you repeat the same workflow with your Version 2 prompt, generate predictions, evaluate them, and calculate the average score for Version 2.

  "{review_text}"
  """

# ZERO-Shot Prompting V2  — Same task, but with brand context & quality constraints
def zero_shot_v2(review_text: str, rating: int) -> str:
    return f"""You are a senior Customer Intelligence Analyst at ChicStyle, a premium women's clothing retailer.
Your task is to analyse customer reviews with high accuracy and generate structured reports.
Accuracy is critical — your outputs will be used by the product and marketing teams.

A customer has left a {rating}-star review. Analyse it carefully and respond in this EXACT format:

Category: <one of: Sizing & Fit | Fabric & Quality | Style & Design | Comfort | Value for Money | Delivery & Service | General Feedback>
Sentiment: <Positive | Neutral | Negative>  (must be consistent with the {rating}-star rating)
Summary: <1 sentence, max 25 words, factual summary of the review>
Personalized Message: <1 warm, brand-appropriate sentence addressed to the customer; do not mention competitors>
Retail Insight: <1 specific, actionable recommendation for the product or operations team>

Customer Review:
\"{review_text}\"

Important: Return ONLY the 5 fields above. No extra commentary.
"""

EXAMPLE 1 — Positive Review (5★):
Review: "Absolutely love this blouse! The fabric is incredibly soft and the color is exactly as pictured. Fits perfectly — I ordered my usual size. Will definitely buy more colors."
---
Category: Fabric & Quality
Sentiment: Positive
Summary: Customer loves the fabric, color accuracy, and true-to-size fit.
Personalized Message: We're so happy you love your new blouse — we'd love to see you in it! 💛
Retail Insight: Highlight fabric softness and color accuracy in product descriptions to set correct expectations.

EXAMPLE 2 — Negative Review (1★):
Review: "This dress is completely unwearable. It arrived with a broken zipper and the seam on the left side was half-open. Returned immediately. Very disappointed."
---
Category: Fabric & Quality

Summary: Dress arrived with a broken zipper and open seam — customer returned it immediately.
Personalized Message: We sincerely apologise for this experience — please contact us and we will resolve this for you right away.
Retail Insight: Implement pre-shipment quality control checks specifically for zippers and seams; this defect should never reach the customer.
"""


def few_shot_v1(review_text: str, rating: int) -> str:

{FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES}

---
"""

Technique 3: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting¶

Questions:

  1. How do you instruct the model to "think step-by-step" internally but only show the final, structured answer?

  2. How can you combine the CoT instruction with more detailed reasoning from the COT V1 prompt to create a powerful CoT V2 prompt?

  3. Does encouraging the model to reason first lead to a measurable improvement in the quality of the generated insights?

How the process works:

  1. First, you create an LLM-as-a-judge function that can evaluate the quality of model outputs.

  2. Then, you run your Prompt Version 1 on a sample of 50 reviews to generate predictions.

  3. You use the judge function to score each prediction and compute the average score for Version 1.

  4. Next, you repeat the same workflow with your Version 2 prompt, generate predictions, evaluate them, and calculate the average score for Version 2.

# CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT V1  — Simple step-by-step instruction

def cot_v1(review_text: str, rating: int) -> str:
    return f"""You are a Customer Intelligence Analyst at ChicStyle.

Think step-by-step through this customer review before writing your final answer.
Only output the final structured answer — do NOT show your thinking.

Steps to follow internally:
1. Read the review carefully.
2. Identify the main topic being discussed (sizing, fabric, delivery, etc.)
3. Assess the overall emotional tone and verify it matches the {rating}-star rating.
4. Summarise what happened in one sentence.
5. Draft an empathetic reply.
6. Think of a specific operational improvement the business could make.

Now write your final answer in this exact format:
Category: ...
Sentiment: ...
Summary: ...
Personalized Message: ...
Retail Insight: ...

Review: \"{review_text}\" (Rating: {rating}/5)
"""

print("Running Chain-of-Thought V1...")
ct_v1_df, ct_v1_avg = run_prompt_pipeline(cot_v1, "CoT V1")
print("\nSample outputs:")
print(ct_v1_df[["Category","Sentiment","Judge_Score"]].head(5).to_string())

 CoT V1 avg judge score = 1.0000

0                 Sizing/Fit      Negative          1.0
1             Fabric Quality      Negative          1.0
2             Sizing and Fit  Disappointed          1.0
3  Sizing and Fabric Quality      Negative          1.0
4                     Sizing      Negative          1.0

Observation

  • By switching to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) V1, the extracted categories have become highly focused on specific operational pain points (e.g., "Sizing/Fit", "Quality Control", "Product Quality and Fit").
  • While the categories are highly descriptive, the vocabulary is becoming completely unstandardized. For example, row 0 uses "Sizing/Fit", while row 2 uses "Sizing and Fit". More importantly, under Sentiment, row 1 introduced an emotion-based label: "Disappointed".

# CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT V2  — Full mental checklist with validation steps

def cot_v2(review_text: str, rating: int) -> str:
    return f"""You are a senior Customer Intelligence Analyst at ChicStyle, a premium women's clothing retailer.
Accuracy and empathy are the top priorities.

Follow this internal reasoning process step by step — but show ONLY the final structured output.

INTERNAL REASONING (do not output this):
Step 1 — READ: What is the customer's main complaint or praise? What specific product attribute do they mention?
Step 2 — CATEGORISE: Which of these 7 categories fits best?
          [Sizing & Fit | Fabric & Quality | Style & Design | Comfort | Value for Money | Delivery & Service | General Feedback]
Step 3 — SENTIMENT: What is the emotional tone? Does it match the {rating}-star rating?
          ({rating}★ → should be {'Positive' if rating >= 4 else 'Neutral' if rating == 3 else 'Negative'})
Step 4 — SUMMARISE: Write a 1-sentence factual summary (max 25 words).
Step 5 — REPLY: Draft a warm, empathetic, brand-appropriate reply. Acknowledge the feeling first.
Step 6 — INSIGHT: What specific operational action should the product or operations team take?
Step 7 — VALIDATE: Check that Sentiment matches the rating. Check all 5 fields are populated.

FINAL OUTPUT (only this section):
Category: ...
Sentiment: ...
Summary: ...
Personalized Message: ...
Retail Insight: ...

Customer Review ({rating}/5 stars):
\"{review_text}\"
"""

print("Running Chain-of-Thought V2...")
ct_v2_df, ct_v2_avg = run_prompt_pipeline(cot_v2, "CoT V2")
print(f"\nCoT  V1 average score : {ct_v1_avg:.4f}")
print(f"CoT  V2 average score : {ct_v2_avg:.4f}")
print(f"Improvement           : {ct_v2_avg - ct_v1_avg:.4f}")

Running Chain-of-Thought V2...
 CoT V2 avg judge score = 0.9920

CoT  V1 average score : 1.0000
CoT  V2 average score : 0.9920
Improvement           : -0.0080

Observation

  • Switching to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) V2 actually caused a drop in performance, resulting in a negative improvement score of -0.0400 compared to V1. This could be the cause of too many rules which very common in Gen AI models.
  • The average judge score dropped below a perfect 1.0 for the first time down to 0.9600

Applying GenAI for Product Recommendation:¶

Now, let's use the model for a different task: predicting the Recommended IND flag.

Questions:

  1. How do you design a prompt that strictly asks for a binary output (1 or 0) and a brief reason?

  2. What kind of function is needed to reliably parse the model's text response to extract the 1/0 flag and the Reason?

  3. How do you evaluate the model's performance as a classifier using standard metrics like accuracy, confusion matrix, and classification report?

How the Process Works

1. Prepare Data

Copy the dataset, store the original recommendation labels, and remove them from the model input to avoid leakage.

2. Generate Predictions

Use a strict two-line prompt to make the LLM output a binary recommendation (1/0) and a short reason based only on the review text.

3. Parse Outputs

Extract the flag and reason from the raw LLM response using regex-based parsing that handles formatting issues.

4. Build Prediction Table

Run the prompt for each review, parse the result, and store the predictions in a new DataFrame.

5. Evaluate Performance

Compare LLM predictions with true labels using accuracy, confusion matrix, and classification report.

6. Explain Mismatches

For incorrect predictions, generate a short explanation describing why the model’s decision may have differed from the human label.

Observations and Insights¶

Refined Insights:

  • What are the most meaningful and recurring insights from the customer reviews, as identified by your best-performing model?
  • Zero-Shot V1 slightly outperformed Zero-Shot V2, with average scores of 1.0000 vs 0.9867, but the difference is minimal and likely not statistically meaningful given the small sample size.
  • Both techniques perform at a similarly high level, suggesting a possible ceiling effect where the task is too easy to clearly separate prompting strategies.
  • V2 shows higher variability, while V1 is the most consistently strong performer.
  • Overall, results indicate that more data or a harder evaluation setup is needed to meaningfully distinguish between techniques.

Generating Actionable Product Improvement Suggestions¶

  • Based on the aggregated insights from your best model, what are 3 short-term (3-6 months) and 3 long-term (6-12 months) actionable business recommendations for the retail company?

  • How does this automated GenAI pipeline solve the initial business problem and create value?

Observations and Insights¶

Short-Term Recommendations (Next 3–6 Months)

  • The model frequently extracted structural anomalies where customers noted that items were "outrageously small" or "boxy and unflattering" relative to standard sizing templates. You should programmatically trigger warning banners on product pages matching those specific Clothing.ID metrics (e.g., "This item runs small in the shoulders; we recommend sizing up"). This immediately reduces sizing-related return rates.
  • Use the automatically created category system to fix messy or inconsistent product labels in the backend. By grouping reviews into clear categories (like separating “Knits,” “Blouses,” and “Dresses”), the merchandising team can repair broken filters and improve search so customers can more easily find products the way they actually talk about them.

Long-Term Recommendations (Next 6–12 Months)

  • Automatically send a custom message to customers who leave low ratings within 24 hours to improve satisfaction and encourage repeat purchases.
  • Combine weekly insights by department so product teams can see trends and improve products over time.

Conclusion¶

This project successfully designed, evaluated, and validated an end-to-end automated Generative AI Text Intelligence Pipeline to transform massive volumes of unstructured, conversational customer reviews into structured, high-value business assets. Using a real-world dataset of 23,486 clothing reviews, the project advanced systematically from exploratory linguistic distributions (Word Clouds) through multiple prompt engineering methodologies (Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought). Finally, an automated quality control layer was implemented using an LLM-as-Judge validation framework to analytically isolate the optimal model candidate for production deployment.
